chapter1.title: The cursor without a mouse
chapter1.text: Tdoay I decided to work out where my time at the computer goes, and to my surprise almost all of it turns out to be spent on tiny and utterly repetitive movements of the mouse, back and forth again.
chapter1.intro: Hello! Let's start at the beginning — with the cursor. Imagine this is your document, and there's a mistake in it.
chapter1.spotTypo: See it? The very first word says “Tdoay” instead of “Today”.
chapter1.trySlow: People usually hunt for it like this: press <keys/> and wait for the cursor to crawl. Try it.
chapter1.tooSlow: The cursor is at the end, the mistake is at the start. That is a long way to hold an arrow.
chapter1.tryFast: There's a far quicker way. Hold <keys/> — the cursor jumps a whole word. Try it.
chapter1.itJumped: The cursor jumped a whole word. Noticeably quicker, isn't it?
chapter1.practise: You can jump right as well — <keys/>. Hop back and forth by words.
chapter1.trySlowDone: See? The cursor moves one character at a time. Slow.
chapter1.fixIt: Jump <keys/> back to the misspelled word and fix it: delete what's wrong and type “Today” correctly.
chapter1.fixedDone: Done. The mistake is gone — and you got to it in a few presses, not a hundred.
chapter1.tryLines: You can move a whole line at a time — <keys/> and <keysAlt/>. Walk up and down.
chapter1.tryLinesDone: Much quicker than stepping through letters.
chapter1.stillSlow: Inside the line though you still crawl one character at a time. And the line is long.

chapter2.title: Edges of the line and the document
chapter2.text:
Dear diary, today I spent half a day hunting for the right spot in a text again.
It turns out the start of a line is one press away.
And so is the start of the whole document.
chapter2.intro: Chapter two. Now let's get to the edges — of a line and of the whole text.
chapter2.tryLineStart: To the start of the line — <keys/>. One press, however many words it holds. Try it.
chapter2.tryLineStartDone: The cursor is at the start of the line.
chapter2.tryLineEnd: To the end of the line — <keys/>. Go back.
chapter2.tryLineEndDone: And back to the end. Two presses put you at either end of the line.
chapter2.wholeText: And what if the text is long and you need its very beginning or very end?
chapter2.docStart: To the top of the document — <keys/>. Try it.
chapter2.docStartDone: You're at the top, on the first line.
chapter2.docEndDone: At the bottom. Two presses cover the whole document, however long it is.
chapter2.practise: And the same for the document — <keys/> and <keysAlt/>.
chapter2.practiseDone: Nicely done. The edges of any text are one press away now.
chapter2.closing: Four moves, and you travel a text of any length instantly.
chapter2.drillLine: Let's drill it: run from one end of the line to the other — <keys/> and <keysAlt/>.
chapter2.drillLineDone: Both ends of a line are one press away now.

chapter3.title: Selecting text
chapter3.text:
Selecting with a mouse is awkward: your hand reaches, aims, drags — and misses by a couple of letters.
So you let go and start again, round and round.
From the keyboard the same thing takes no aiming at all.
chapter3.intro: Chapter three. Now let's look at selecting text. Good news: there are no new shortcuts at all.
chapter3.tryChar: The whole secret is one key — Shift. Hold it and press what you already know: <keys/>.
chapter3.tryCharDone: See? The cursor moves and drags the selection along.
chapter3.tryEdge: And to the ends of the line — <keys/> and <keysAlt/>. It selects either way.
chapter3.tryEdgeDone: A line selects both ways in a single move.
chapter3.closing: That's the entire rule: Shift turns any movement into a selection. Nothing new, just one extra key.
chapter3.deleteIt: A selection is erased with one key — <keys/>.
chapter3.deleteItDone: Gone. Select and erase — two moves instead of holding the key down.
chapter3.selectAll: One last thing: select the whole text at once — <keys/>.
chapter3.selectAllDone: The whole document selected in one press.
chapter3.wipeAll: Everything is selected, so erase it all at once: <keys/>. That's how you clear a document.
chapter3.wipeAllDone: Empty. Two keys and a blank page.

chapter4.title: Editing and undoing
chapter4.text:
This morning I had coffee strong and sat down to sort out my inbox.
So many letters had piled up that I finished the cup before I reached the middle of the list.
chapter4.intro: Chapter four. Let's learn to move text from place to place.
chapter4.pasteIt: Paste it — <keys/> — and add a space so the words don't run together.
chapter4.pasteItDone: “Strong coffee”. The words are where they belong, and no mouse was needed.
chapter4.undoItDone: The text rolled back. Undo remembers many steps, not one.
chapter4.redoIt: And if you undid too much, bring it back: <keys/>.
chapter4.redoItDone: Back again. You can walk your edits forwards and backwards.
chapter4.cutIt: Cutting is the same, except the word goes: <keys/>. Select “strong” again and cut it.
chapter4.closing: Done. Select, cut, paste, undo, redo, erase a word — all under your fingers.
chapter4.spot: Look: “coffee strong” — the words are the wrong way round, it should be “strong coffee”. Hop by words (<keys/> and <keysAlt/>) and stop right after “strong”.
chapter4.cutItDone: The word is gone and sitting on the clipboard.
chapter4.deleteWord: You can erase without selecting too: <keys/> takes out a whole word. Try it.
chapter4.deleteWordDone: A word per press. No more erasing one letter at a time.
chapter4.tidySpace: The word is on the clipboard, but it left two spaces behind. Delete the extra one — <keys/>.
chapter4.tidySpaceDone: Tidy. Cutting a word always leaves spaces to clean up.
chapter4.copyIt: Copying first: <keys/> puts the selection on the clipboard and leaves it alone. Select the word and copy it.
chapter4.copyItDone: Copied. The text is still there, a copy is on the clipboard.
chapter4.spotDone: In place — the caret is right after the word.

chapter5.title: The workshop
chapter5.text:
Tomorow I'm going into town for groceries.
I'll get bread fresh, some milk and a bit of cheese.
I'll probably pick up something for tea as well.
chapter5.intro: Chapter five, the last one. The workshop: you do the work here, I barely help.
chapter5.fixTypo: Three things need fixing in this note, and I'm not lighting up keys any more — you know all of this. First: the very first word has a typo. Find it and fix it.
chapter5.swap: Second: the second line says “bread fresh”. Swap the words so it reads “fresh bread”.
chapter5.swapDone: Nicely done. Select, cut, move — exactly as in the last chapter.
chapter5.dropLine: Third: the last line doesn't belong. Delete the whole thing.
chapter5.dropLineDone: Clean. The note is in order.
chapter5.closing: That's it. You found a typo, swapped words and cut what didn't belong — without once reaching for the mouse. From here it becomes habit on its own.

page0.title: The city on foot
page0.body:
Morning in a city begins before the city itself wakes up. The pavements have already been swept, and the first coffee shops are only now switching on their signs.

Leave half an hour early and walk at least part of the way, and the city turns into something else entirely. It turns out there is a passage between two streets you have known for years, and behind it a small garden you have driven past a thousand times without once seeing it.

On foot you see everything at eye level. Not whole facades, but doors, signs, steps, cats in windows. It is not the city on the postcards, but it is the one you remember.

Morning suits this best. By day the city hurries and shoves; by evening it is tired. In the morning it has not yet decided what sort of day to have, and so it is unusually friendly.

Start small: get off one stop early. One stop is ten minutes on foot and a piece of the city you knew nothing about.

A month later you will know your own city better than in all the years before it, and you will know that morning is the best part of the day.

The surprising part is that none of it needs planning. No route, no destination, no app to count your steps and congratulate you on them. It is enough to go out and turn the wrong way.

A city is built in layers. The first is the one you drive along: avenues, bridges, junctions. The second is the lanes a car will not fit down. The third is the courtyards, where the washing hangs and other people's bicycles lean. From the third layer a city looks like somebody's home rather than a diagram.

In winter it works better still. Fewer people, shorter sounds, windows lit earlier. Fifteen minutes in the cold wakes you more thoroughly than any coffee and costs less.

There is a plainly practical gain too. A walking person thinks better than a sitting one: half the problems you fought with all of yesterday solve themselves between two junctions. It is not mysterious, it is only rhythm.

Not everywhere, of course, and not every day. But if two of your five working days begin with twenty minutes on foot, the difference shows by the end of the second week. And it is not really about health: it is that the morning stops being a commute and becomes part of the day.

Try it tomorrow. Leaving early is hard only the first time — after that the city starts calling, and at some point you notice you are walking not because it is good for you but because it is nicer.

browser1.title: Tabs
browser1.intro: Chapter one. This is a browser — where most of the day happens. We start with tabs.
browser1.open: A new tab opens with <keys/>. Try it.
browser1.openDone: There it is, right next to the one you were on.
browser1.whereItWent: Notice: the caret is already in the address bar. The browser is waiting for you to type.
browser1.openMoreDone: Several now. Let us close the spare ones.
browser1.oops: Now imagine you closed it by accident. And it had a half-written letter in it.
browser1.reopen: No matter: <keys/> brings back the last tab you closed. Ten of them, if you like.
browser1.reopenDone: Back again. This one will save your evening some day.
browser1.drill: Let us make it stick. Open and close tabs — <keys/> and <keysAlt/>.
browser1.drillDone: Good. Three shortcuts you will use every single day.
browser1.closing: Tabs are under your fingers now: open one, close one, and — best of all — bring back the one you closed by mistake.

browser2.title: Moving between tabs
browser2.intro: Chapter two. There are a lot of tabs now, and the more there are the narrower they get.
browser2.next: The next tab is <keys/>. Go all the way round.
browser2.nextDone: You reached the end and came back to the start. Tabs go round in a circle.
browser2.drillDone: Remember this pair: it works the same in every browser on every system.
browser2.digits: But one at a time is slow. Tabs are numbered from the left, and you can jump straight to any of them.
browser2.thirdDone: Straight there. The digits one to eight all work like that.
browser2.last: Nine is the odd one out: it is always the last tab, however many there are. Try <keys/>.
browser2.lastDone: The far right one. Even with twenty tabs open.
browser2.closing: Tabs no longer need catching with a mouse, however many of them there are.

browser3.title: The address bar
browser3.intro: Chapter three. The most frequent mouse click of anybody's day is on the address bar. It need not be.
browser3.focus: <keys/> — and the caret is in the address.
browser3.focusDone: There it is. And here is the part that matters...
browser3.selected: The whole address is selected. Everything the first course taught you about selections holds here: type straight over it, nothing needs erasing.
browser3.typeDone: Good. Now press <enter/> and the browser will open the page.
browser3.arrived: That is how you open a site whose address you know. But the address bar is a search box too: when you do not know the address, just type what you are after.
browser3.again: Once more, to make it stick: <keys/>.
browser3.againDone: That is all there is to it. No more aiming a mouse at the address bar.
browser3.closing: The address bar needs no mouse any more: one shortcut and you are typing.
browser3.tip: And two small discoveries. You never need to type www or http:// at the front — the browser fills that in. And case makes no difference: WEATHER.COM, Weather.com and weather.com are the same address.

browser4.title: Find on the page
browser4.intro: Chapter four. A long article, and the word you want is somewhere in the middle. Most people hunt for it with their eyes.
browser4.openDone: The find box is open with the caret in it.
browser4.typeDone: Look: the browser has highlighted every match and counted them.
browser4.next: To the next match — <keys/>. Walk through them.
browser4.nextDone: The page scrolls itself to each one in turn.
browser4.prev: Back through the matches — <keys/>. The same way in reverse.
browser4.closing: No more hunting for a word by eye: the browser finds every match and counts them for you.

browser5.title: The page and history
browser5.intro: Chapter five. The easy part is left: turning the page. The mouse wheel is not needed for it.
browser5.down: One screen down — <keys/>. Turn a few pages.
browser5.downDone: Exactly one screen, not however far a flick of the wheel happens to go.
browser5.upDone: That is how long articles get read.
browser5.ends: All the way down and all the way up — <keys/> and <keysAlt/>. The same shortcuts that took you to the ends of a text in the first course. Have a wander.
browser5.endsDone: The same keys as in the first course — here they turn the page.
browser5.back: Now history. Back to the previous page — <keys/>.
browser5.backDone: The same arrow button, without the mouse.
browser5.closing: Screen by screen, to the top, to the bottom, back through history — and never a mouse wheel.

browser6.title: The workshop
browser6.intro: Chapter six, the last. No more prompting: I say what needs doing, you remember how.
browser6.oops: Ah, a mistake. Bring it back.
browser6.oopsDone: There it is — the shortcut this whole course was for.
browser6.find: Find the word “morning” on this page.
browser6.back: Go back to the previous page.
browser6.jump: And to finish: jump to the last tab in one move.
browser6.closing: Not one prompt, and it all worked. Which means the shortcuts are in your fingers now, not on a list.
browser6.tidy: Tidy up after yourself: close the find bar.

Status:
app1.intro: Chapter one. In front of you is a document in an ordinary application. Everything that follows works the same in an editor, in mail and in a spreadsheet.
app1.dot: Look at the title bar: there is a dot beside the name. It means the document has changed and those changes have not been saved yet.
app1.saveDone: A dialog: the document has no name yet, and the application is asking for one.
app1.named: The name is already selected — just like the address bar. Type over it, no need to erase.
app1.name: Report
app1.tabDone: The ring moved to the checkbox. That is how Tab walks any dialog: one field after another.
app1.space: A checkbox is switched with the space bar — <keys/>.
app1.spaceDone: Switched. Space ticks and unticks any box — but only while the caret is not in a text field.
app1.accept: Confirm — <keys/>. That key always presses the blue button.
app1.gone: And the dot in the title went out: the disk now holds what the screen does.
app1.touch: The note is unfinished — there is nothing after “Status:”. Type the word “urgent”.
app1.touchDone: The dot is back — there is something to save again.
app1.againDone: No dialog this time: the document has a name, so the application simply wrote the file.
app1.saveAs: And if you need a second copy under a different name — <keys/>.
app1.saveAsDone: The same dialog, asking for a new name.
app1.cancelDone: The dialog closed and nothing changed. Escape cancels any dialog.
app1.closing: A dot in the title, a dialog with a name in it, Tab between fields, Space on a checkbox, Enter and Escape at the end. All of it turns up again and again.

app2.title: New, open, print
app2.text:
A couple of lines, so there is something to work with.
Nothing important here.
app2.intro: Chapter two. Every program has a File menu — and you do not have to go into it with the mouse.
app2.blank: It has no name yet: the dot appears the moment you write something.
app2.openDone: A list of files, with the caret on the first.
app2.pickDone: The arrows walk a list exactly as they walk lines of text. Nothing new.
app2.enterDone: The file opened in the same window.
app2.printDone: The print dialog. Enter would send the sheet to the printer.
app2.escape: We have no printer here, so put the dialog away — <keys/>.
app2.close: Close the document — <keys/>. The same key that closed a tab in the browser.
app2.closeDone: The document is closed and the window stayed.
app2.quit: And the last one, the one people most often do not know: <keys/> closes not the document but the whole application. Go ahead and press it — nothing will happen here, because this one keystroke is caught.
app2.quitDone: Nothing closed — but in any other program that would have taken the window and the application with it.
app2.closing: New, open, print, close — and the menu was never needed.

app3.title: Zoom
app3.text: Small print is an everyday thing: a contract, somebody else's slides, an article on an unfamiliar site. You do not have to squint at it.
app3.intro: Chapter three. The size of the text is changed from the keyboard, and almost everywhere in the same way.
app3.in: Bigger — <keys/>. Press it a few times.
app3.outDone: That is as small as it goes.
app3.everywhere: These three work in the browser, in mail, in an editor, in maps. And zero always means “as it was”.
app3.closing: Small print is no longer a reason to lean in: two keys change the size and a third puts it back.

app4.title: The workshop
app4.text:
A note with a few things to do to it.
No keys are named from here on.
app4.intro: Chapter four. No more help: nothing named and nothing lit.
app4.save: Save this note under the name “Letter”.
app4.name: Letter
app4.saveDone: Saved, and the dot in the title went out.
app4.open: Now open the file called Draft letter.
app4.bigger: Rather small. Make the text bigger.
app4.away: And put that dialog away without printing.
app4.closing: Not one key named — and all of it worked.
